children: Lean hog futures on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange (CME) fell to life-of-contract lows on Tuesday, pressured by weak cash hog prices and a slump in wholesale pork prices, traders said.
The US Department of Agriculture priced pork carcasses on Tuesday afternoon at $66.44 per hundredweight, down $2.80 from Monday and the lowest reading in more than six years.

Similarly, the CME's Lean Hog Index (.IHX), a two-day weighted average of cash hog prices, was last quoted at 57.16 cents per pound, its lowest value since August 2020, reflecting weak demand from meat packers.

"Hogs seemingly remain ample. And going into Thanksgiving, it isn't going to be any better because packers will have a short slaughter week next week," said Doug Houghton, analyst with Brock Capital Management.

On the CME, December lean hog futures (LHZ26) settled down 2.250 cents at 53.100 cents per pound after notching a contract low at 52.825 cents. February lean hogs (LHG27) ended down 2.350 cents at 58.325 cents a pound after hitting a contract low at 58.250 cents.
In the cattle market, CME live cattle futures fell for a second day on technical selling after a 3.5% climb last week in the benchmark February
fell 1.550 cents to 218.775 cents per pound and February cattle
fell 4.900 cents to settle at 328.200 cents per pound.

Ahead of the USDA's monthly feedlot data on Friday, analysts surveyed by Reuters, on average, expect the government to report the number of US cattle on feed as of November 1 at 11.671 million head, or 99.7% of last year's total.
Analysts, on average, estimated placements into feedlots during October at 97% of year-earlier levels, and October marketings at 94.9% of levels seen a year ago.
